quotes.name: Gloria Liu
quotes.quote: A one-point drop on a scale like that — I'll be honest, it doesn't change what happens in the building on Monday morning. The kids still come in, the teachers still teach, and I still walk the halls. The district watches that number, sure, but I watch the kids. If anything, a dip like that makes me look closer at where we might be slipping — maybe it's a cohort thing, maybe it's a resource thing — but it doesn't mean I'm suddenly going to pull books off shelves or cut a program. We're still the strongest school in the city, and that's not because of a number. It's because of the people here.

quotes.name: Maya Torres-Dillon
quotes.quote: Honestly, I read that 75% as both. It's a strength we should be proud of — that's a real number, and it means most of our kids are leaving ready for what's next. But if I'm being honest with you, as a teacher, I don't get to treat any number as a finish line. That 8.53 slipping, even a little, that's the kind of thing that gets my attention. It's not about panicking over a decimal point. It's about asking what that one student who just enrolled needs, and whether we're actually serving every kid in that building, not just the ones already on track. We've got the strongest record in the city, and that's something to protect — but the day we start thinking we've arrived is the day we stop pushing.

quotes.name: Mei Wong
quotes.quote: Honestly, I can't speak to the enrollment numbers or the per-student funding figure — that's not something I see in my day-to-day. What I can tell you is what I see at pickup: parents asking if their kid ate a real snack, teachers who remember every child's name, and a community that shows up. If the index slipped a little, I wouldn't be surprised if it's because we're all stretched thinner, not because the kids or the staff care any less.
